ktb.candidate_root_contribution: Consigning/fixing something into a determinate, standing inscription — setting a content down so that it holds as an established, binding record. The residue is "fixed inscribed standing," which surfaces concretely as marks-set-down (writing, recording) and figuratively as an ordinance-set-as-binding (decree/prescription/assigned term), the latter carried by the internal metaphor of inscribing an obligation.
ktb.plain_explanation: Across all 319 confirmed occurrences the root ك ت ب contributes one thing: fixing a content into a settled, inscribed standing. This shows up in five internally-observable families. (1) Physical/registrational writing: angels/messengers who يَكْتُبُونَ what people plot (10:21; 43:80; 82:11 كَٰتِبِينَ), نَكْتُبُ مَا قَدَّمُوا (36:12), scribes writing a debt-contract فَٱكْتُبُوهُ (2:282, eight verbal/participial tokens), writing on tablets وَكَتَبْنَا لَهُۥ فِى ٱلْأَلْوَاحِ (7:145), forgers who يَكْتُبُونَ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ بِأَيْدِيهِمْ (2:79), copying out ٱكْتَتَبَهَا (25:5, Form VIII). (2) The revealed Scripture: the dominant noun sense الْكِتَٰب — تِلْكَ ءَايَٰتُ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ (10:1 etc.), ذَٰلِكَ ٱلْكِتَٰبُ (2:2), the Book given to Moses/Muhammad, أَهْلِ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ. (3) The record/register: كِتَٰبًا يَلْقَىٰهُ مَنشُورًا (17:13), أُوتِىَ كِتَٰبَهُۥ بِيَمِينِهِ (17:71), وَوُضِعَ ٱلْكِتَٰبُ (18:49), كِتَٰبٍ مُّبِينٍ = the fixed record of all things (10:61; 11:6; 27:75). (4) The decree/prescription: كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلصِّيَامُ/ٱلْقِصَاصُ/ٱلْقِتَالُ (2:183; 2:178; 2:216; 2:246; 4:77; 3:154), كَتَبَ عَلَىٰ نَفْسِهِ ٱلرَّحْمَةَ (6:12,54), كَتَبَ فِى قُلُوبِهِمُ ٱلْإِيمَٰنَ (58:22), مَا كَتَبَ ٱللَّهُ لَنَا (9:51), كَتَبَ ٱللَّهُ لَأَغْلِبَنَّ (58:21). (5) The appointed/fixed instrument: an assigned term حَتَّىٰ يَبْلُغَ ٱلْكِتَٰبُ أَجَلَهُۥ (2:235), لِكُلِّ أَجَلٍ كِتَابٌ (13:38), كِتَابٌ مَّعْلُومٌ (15:4); a letter/missive بِّكِتَٰبِى هَٰذَا (27:28), كِتَٰبٌ كَرِيمٌ (27:29); a written emancipation-contract يَبْتَغُونَ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ / فَكَاتِبُوهُمْ (24:33). In every family, once the form and construction are subtracted, the same core remains: something is fixed into a standing inscribed determination.
ktb.strongest_counterexample: The passive-decree cluster كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلْقِصَاصُ / ٱلصِّيَامُ / ٱلْقِتَالُ (2:178; 2:183; 2:216; 2:246; 4:77; 3:154 كُتِبَ عَلَيْهِمُ ٱلْقَتْلُ). Here nothing is literally written and the surface meaning is pure obligation, so the "inscription" residue looks absent — this is the hardest case for a single fixing-into-inscription contribution. It reconciles because the obligation vector is supplied by the construction (passive + عَلَىٰ = "binding upon"), while the ROOT is what renders that obligation a fixed, standing decree rather than a passing command; the same idiom is shown internally to be inscriptional when the object is interiorized — كَتَبَ فِى قُلُوبِهِمُ ٱلْإِيمَٰنَ (58:22) uses the identical verb for "inscribed faith in their hearts," confirming that كُتِبَ عَلَىٰ is the inscribe-as-binding metaphor, not a separate homonymous "obligate." A close second is مَا كَتَبَ ٱللَّهُ لَنَا (9:51), where the fixed decree of fate is conceived as what God has "written for us."

slm.candidate_root_contribution: UNBREACHED WHOLENESS / INTACTNESS — a thing being free of breach, defect, harm or division — together with its dynamic projection: the RENDERING-OVER of something in its whole, intact state. This single residue surfaces statically (something is sound/whole/unharmed) and transitively (something whole is handed over / given up entire).
slm.plain_explanation: Across almost the whole packet, س ل م contributes the idea of a thing being WHOLE and unbreached — free of harm, flaw, or division — and, when active, of that whole thing being handed over intact. The greeting/eschatological سَلَام cluster (10:10, 13:24, 19:15, 19:33, 37:79-181, 36:58, 56:26, 97:5, 6:54, 7:46, 16:32, 33:44, 39:73, 43:89, 50:34, 15:46, and the reticent قالوا سلاما of 11:69, 15:52, 25:63, 51:25) is 'wholeness/safety be upon you' — an unbreached state wished or realized. الله السَّلام (59:23) is the Flawless/Whole. دار/سبل السلام (6:127, 10:25, 5:16) is the destination of intactness. سَلِيم قلب (26:89, 37:84) and سالِمون (68:43) are the sound/unharmed self. On the transitive side, أسلم وجهه لله (2:112, 3:20, 4:125, 31:22, 6:14, 6:71, 40:66) and مُسْلِم / إسلام (the large N(IV)/PN(IV) mass) are giving one's whole self over intact to God; مُستسلمون (37:26) is that same giving-over in defeat; ألقوا السَّلم (16:28, 16:87, 4:90-91) is laying oneself/one's arms down whole; السِّلم/السَّلم (2:208, 8:61, 47:35) is entering an unbreached, non-hostile state. Form II carries the handing-over-intact sense literally: سلّمتم ما آتيتم 'you hand over in full' (2:233), دية مُسَلَّمة 'blood-money paid over entire' (4:92), بقرة مُسَلَّمة 'a cow sound/without blemish' (2:71), الله سَلَّم 'God kept whole/delivered' (8:43), and رجلاً سَلَمًا لرجل 'a man belonging wholly/undivided to one master' (39:29). تسليماً (4:65, 33:22, 33:56) is whole, unreserved submission. The same thread — intactness, or something rendered whole — runs through all of these.
slm.strongest_counterexample: سُلَّم 'ladder' at 6:35 (أو سُلَّمًا في السماء — 'or a ladder into the sky') and 52:38 (أم لهم سُلَّمٌ يستمعون فيه — 'or have they a ladder by which they eavesdrop'). Both are instrument nouns (فُعَّل) denoting a means of ascent to heaven. Nothing in either verse's internal evidence displays wholeness, soundness, safety, or handing-over; the only way to attach the candidate residue ('a means that conveys one up intact') is by importing external etymology, which the hard rules forbid as evidence. From internal Quranic evidence alone the residue is NOT demonstrably present here, so these two occurrences resist the proposed universal contribution.

Hkm.candidate_root_contribution: The root contributes the notion of bringing a matter to a FIRM, AUTHORITATIVE, DECISIVE settlement — fixing/binding something soundly so that it holds and rival options or corruption are barred. The residue is not "knowledge" and not "separation"; it is the act/quality/faculty/agency of decisive determination that makes a thing firm and settled.
Hkm.plain_explanation: Across all 210 confirmed occurrences the root's steady contribution is "decisive, firm, authoritative settling of a matter." Surface variety is carried by FORM and CONSTRUCTION, not by the root: (1) Form I verb yaHkumu / iHkum = to render the settlement, overwhelmingly with the construction bayna-hum ("judge/decide BETWEEN" disputants) or bi-... ("decide BY/WITH" a norm: bi-l-Haqq, bi-l-qisT, bi-maa anzala llaah) — e.g. 5:42, 5:48, 4:105, 38:26, 2:213, 16:124, 39:3, 22:69; (2) taHkumuun "how do you decide/determine?" carries the same act, usually in rebuke of arbitrary determinations (37:154; 68:36; saaʔa maa yaHkumuun 16:59, 29:4, 45:21, 6:136); (3) Form II Hakkama = CAUSE someone to be the decider, "make you arbiter" (4:65; 5:43); (4) Form VI yataHaakamuu = mutually SEEK a decider's settlement (4:60, to Taghut); (5) Form IV (uHkimat 11:1; yuHkimu 22:52) and participle muHkam(aat/-ah) (3:7; 47:20) = render/made FIRM, decisive, unambiguous — the clearest internal anchor of the "firm-fixing" residue, since muHkamaat stand opposed to mutashaabihaat; (6) noun Hukm = the binding determination/authority itself ("the Hukm belongs to God alone" 12:40, 12:67, 6:57, 40:12; "to Him belongs the Hukm" 28:70, 28:88, 6:62); (7) Hukm as a God-given endowment of sound decisive discernment to prophets (12:22, 21:74, 21:79, 26:83, 19:12, 3:79, 6:89, 45:16); (8) Hikma "wisdom" = the FACULTY that yields sound firm determinations, taught alongside the Book (2:129, 2:151, 3:48, 62:2, 2:269, 16:125, 31:12); (9) agent nouns Hakam "arbiter" (6:114, 4:35), Hukkaam "rulers/judges" (2:188), Haakimiin / khayr al-Haakimiin / aHkam al-Haakimiin "deciders / best-and-most-decisive of deciders" (7:87, 10:109, 11:45, 95:8); (10) adjective Hakiim "all-wise / firmly-decreeing," as a divine epithet (usually paired ʕaziiz Hakiim, ʕaliim Hakiim) and of the Book (al-kitaab al-Hakiim 10:1, 31:2; al-qurʔaan al-Hakiim 36:2) and of "a decisively-decreed matter" (amr Hakiim 44:4). Subtract form and construction and the same core remains everywhere: decisive, firm, authoritative determination.
Hkm.strongest_counterexample: The largest strain is the Hikma "wisdom" cluster and the fixed epithet Hakiim. In 16:125 (adʕu ... bi-l-Hikma wa-l-mawʕiZa l-Hasana), 2:151 / 3:48 / 62:2 / 5:110 (teaching "the Book and al-Hikma"), and 2:269 (yuʔti l-Hikmata man yashaaʔ), "wisdom" surfaces as a taught content or manner of address, where no overt act of adjudication is present — the decisive-determination residue survives only as the underlying FACULTY of sound firm discernment, an agentive/metonymic extension of the bare act. Likewise the 84 Hakiim tokens as a near-formulaic divine epithet (ʕaziiz Hakiim, ʕaliim Hakiim) could, taken alone, be read as generic "wise." These are reconciled — not forced — because the same corpus internally fixes Hakiim to the decisive-firm sense via amr Hakiim (44:4, "a decisively-decreed matter") and via the muHkamaat/muHkama firmness cluster (3:7; 47:20; 11:1; 22:52), and because Hakiim is repeatedly held DISTINCT from knowledge by pairing (Hakiim + ʕaliim, Hakiim + khabiir), so its own contribution cannot collapse into "knowing."

Elm.candidate_root_contribution: Candidate residue: "cognition — the mind's grasp/hold of a determinate fact, and by extension the determinate-thing-that-is-known and the act of causing it to be known." After subtracting form, this residue is directly visible in the overwhelming mass of occurrences: Form I/V verbs ʿalima/yaʿlamu/taʿallama = "to know / come to know / learn" (100:9 "does he not know", 102:3-5 "you will come to know", 2:102 "they learn"); the ADJ/intensive ʿalīm / aʿlam = "All-Knowing / more-knowing" (the property of knowing, ~150 occ); the abstract noun ʿilm / al-ʿilm = "knowledge, the known content" (102:5 ʿilm al-yaqīn, ~110 occ); Form II ʿallama + muʿallam = "to teach / one taught" (2:31 "He taught Adam", 44:14 "a taught madman", 42 occ — Form II supplies causation, the residue supplies the knowing that is caused); and the passive participle maʿlūm = "known / appointed / determinate" (yawm/maqām/ajal/ḥaqq maʿlūm — 15:38, 37:164, 70:24 — the thing fixed BECAUSE known/specified, ~11 occ). Across these ~776 occurrences the cognition residue is non-empty, distinctive, and demonstrably present in every verse cited.
Elm.plain_explanation: The root ع ل م is the Qur'an's "knowing" root and it saturates ~776 of its 854 occurrences with one stable core: to hold a fact in the mind (know), the one who does so (the Knower / All-Knowing), the content held (knowledge), the causing of another to hold it (teach), and the thing that is fixed because it is known (appointed/determinate). That core is clean and universal across the whole cognition family. BUT the packet also assigns to this same root two occurrence-islands that do NOT display the knowing residue on the verse evidence alone: (1) al-ʿālamīn "the worlds / all creatures / all peoples" — 76 occurrences, the fixed phrase rabb al-ʿālamīn "Lord of the worlds" (1:2, 21:107, 26:16...) and "preferred over the worlds" (2:47) — where the text shows only "created realms / nations," with no cognition content; and (2) kal-aʿlām "like the mountains/landmarks," describing ships in the sea (42:32, 55:24) — where the sense is a prominent physical marker, not a mental act. Reconciling these to "knowing" requires the classical etymology (ʿālam = "that by which the Maker is known"; ʿalam = "a mark by which a thing is recognized"), which is lexicon/tafsir — barred as evidence here. From the occurrences alone, these 78 do not carry the residue, so a single distinctive contribution present in EVERY occurrence cannot be established without forcing.
Elm.strongest_counterexample: al-ʿālamīn "the worlds" (76 occ), archetype rabb al-ʿālamīn "Lord of the worlds" (1:2), and "I preferred you over the worlds" (2:47), plus kal-aʿlām "like the mountains/landmarks" for ships at sea (42:32, 55:24). In none of these does the verse text exhibit any act, faculty, or content of knowing. "Worlds/all-creatures/nations" is a cosmological/collective sense; "landmark-mountains" is a physical-marker sense. The cognition residue is simply not present on the evidence; it can only be inserted by importing the disallowed etymology that ʿālam/ʿalam derive from "a sign by which something is known." Per the hard rule, one irreconcilable occurrence defeats universal presence — here there are 78.

Amn.candidate_root_contribution: The root ء-م-ن contributes a single relational state: TRUST-SECURITY — being free from fear/danger because something or someone is relied upon as dependable. This one residue surfaces as: (a) the fear-free condition itself (amn, aaminiin, amanah = security-drowsiness, ma'man = place of safety); (b) the quality of being relied-upon (amiin = trustworthy, al-amaanah = a thing placed in trust); (c) the act of taking-as-trust (Form VIII i'tamana, 2:283 iu'tumina amaanatahu); (d) the intransitive being-secure/trusting (Form I amina: 7:97-99 afa-amina... = do they feel secure from God's stratagem; 12:11 laa ta'mannaa = you do not trust us); and (e) Form IV as the factitive/causative of that state, which is where the two surface senses branch by CONSTRUCTION, not by root: aamana + direct object + min = CONFER security (106:4 wa-aamanahum min khawf = He gave them security from fear; 59:23 al-Mu'min = the Granter-of-security among God's names), while aamana + bi = GRANT one's trust/reliance to, i.e. believe (put one's security in X by affirming it dependable). Faith (iimaan) is thus trust-reliance, and belief and safety are two applications of one trust-security core.
Amn.plain_explanation: Every form of this root is about security-through-trust: feeling safe, being trustworthy, entrusting, or placing your trust/faith in something. Form I "amina" = to feel safe / to trust. Nouns give security (amn), a trust/deposit (amaanah), a trustworthy person (amiin), a safe place (ma'man). Form VIII "i'tamana" = to entrust. Form IV "aamana" is the causative: with min it means "make safe / grant security" (106:4 "gave them security from fear"; God's name al-Mu'min the Security-Giver), and with bi it means "believe in" — which is grammatically the same act of extending trust/reliance to something you hold dependable. So the 537 belief-verbs and 260 believer/faith-nouns are not a separate meaning; they are trust-reliance, the same core that produces amn (safety) and amaanah (trust).
Amn.strongest_counterexample: The belief-cluster (V(IV) aamanuu / N(IV) al-mu'miniin, ~797 tokens) superficially reads as "faith," a sense with no obvious "security" content, and could look like a second, unrelated meaning of the root. This is the one place universal presence could break. It is reconciled by three internal bridges within the packet itself: (1) 106:4 wa-aamanahum min khawf places the SAME Form IV verb in an unambiguous "grant security from fear" reading; (2) 59:23 al-Mu'min lists Form IV participle as a divine name of security-giving beside al-Salaam; (3) 12:17 wa-maa anta bi-mu'min lanaa uses the believer-participle to mean "you will not credit/trust us" — bare trust, no doctrinal "faith." These show the belief tokens are trust-reliance (aamana bi = entrust one's security to), i.e. the identical residue, so the counterexample does not survive.

kfr.candidate_root_contribution: Root residue = "to cover over / screen something so it is occluded from acknowledgement." The root supplies an act of COVERING-OVER applied to some object; what is covered and the valence are set by form/construction/context, not by the root. Cover the truth/signs/lordship of God -> refusal to acknowledge (disbelief); cover a bestowed benefit (niʿma/anʿum) -> non-acknowledgement (ingratitude); (Form II) God covers over evil deeds -> effaces/expiates them; a kaffāra is an act that covers an offense; and in 57:20/48:29 the substantive al-kuffār are the SOWERS — those who cover seed in the soil. One image (occlusion/screening) underlies all 525.
kfr.plain_explanation: The three-letter root k-f-r means, at bottom, to put a cover over something. Everything the Quran does with it is a version of covering: covering up God's truth and signs so you act as if they aren't there (this is what English translates as "disbelief"), covering up a gift so you don't acknowledge it (ingratitude — often explicitly against God's "niʿma"), God covering over people's sins so they are wiped away (the Form II "kaffara ʿan-hum sayyiʾāti-him" verses), an expiation (kaffāra) that covers an offence, and — most tellingly — the farmers/sowers called "al-kuffār" in 57:20 because they cover seed with earth. So the harsh theological sense and the humble farming sense are the same act pointed at different objects.
kfr.strongest_counterexample: The Form II expiation cluster (2:271; 3:193; 3:195; 4:31; 5:12; 5:65; 8:29; 29:7; 39:35; 47:2; 48:5; 64:9; 65:5; 66:8) and the sower reading of al-kuffār in 57:20 (and 48:29) run OPPOSITE in valence to the dominant disbelief sense: God covering sins is favourable, and farmers covering seed is neutral/agricultural, whereas covering God's truth is condemned. If the root meant "disbelieve/deny," these would be genuine breaks. They are not: in "yukaffiru ʿan-hum sayyiʾāti-him" the act is literally to cover the sins over, and in "aʿjaba l-kuffāra nabātu-hu" the kuffār are precisely coverers-of-seed. The residue "cover over" is present in both; only the object and the evaluative valence (supplied by Form II / context) differ. So the hardest cases confirm rather than falsify the unity. Secondary hard case 21:94 "fa-lā kufrāna li-saʿyi-hi" = no covering-over (denial/withholding of acknowledgement) of his effort — also reconciles.

SbH.candidate_root_contribution: The root ص ب ح contributes reference to al-Subh: the day's bright-light phase and, above all, its ONSET — the breaking-forth of whitish daylight that ends the dark of night. This single residue is instantiated three ways across the packet after form is subtracted: (i) the phase/time itself (nouns الصُّبْح, صَبَاح, الإِصْبَاح, adverbial صُبْحًا, participle مُصْبِحِين); (ii) a source that gives that phase's kind of light (the مِفْعَال instrument noun مِصْبَاح / مَصَابِيح 'lamp(s)'); (iii) the ENTRY into that phase, which Form IV أَصْبَحَ ('to reach/enter the morning') grammaticalizes into 'to come to be'. The distinctive core is not generic light and not generic becoming, but the daybreak — the arrival of morning brightness.
SbH.plain_explanation: Every one of the 45 occurrences points back to 'morning / the coming of daylight'. The plainest cases are the dawn-nouns (الصبح 'the dawn' in 11:81, 74:34, 81:18; صباح 'morning' in 37:177; الإصباح 'daybreak' in 6:96), the 'at-daybreak' participle مصبحين (15:66, 15:83, 37:137, 68:17, 68:21), the adverbial صبحاً 'at dawn' (100:3), and صبّحهم 'he came upon them in the morning' (54:38). A large block of أصبح verbs are dawn-destruction reports where morning is transparently the moment of ruin ('and by morning they lay dead in their homes' — 7:78, 7:91, 11:67, 11:94, 29:37; الصيحة … مصبحين 15:83; فأصبحت كالصريم 68:20). Two clusters strain the reading: the LAMP words مصباح/مصابيح (24:35 x2, 41:12, 67:5), where the surviving residue is the bright LIGHT (a lamp is the instrument of morning-like light) rather than the time; and the fully bleached copular أصبح 'became' (e.g. 3:103 'you became brothers', 41:23 'you became of the losers', 5:52/5:53/49:6 'they/you became regretful/losers'), where context shows no dawn at all and only the 'come-to-be' aspect remains. Both are reconcilable through a prototype: the root always names the bright daytime-light phase, given either as light (lamp) or as onset (become) — but in these two clusters the morning-invariant is present by lexical/grammatical inheritance, not visibly in the verse.
SbH.strongest_counterexample: 3:103 — فَأَصْبَحْتُم بِنِعْمَتِهِۦٓ إِخْوَٰنًا ('by His grace you became brothers'). There is no dawn, no morning marker, and no light in the context; أصبح functions as a pure inchoative copula ('came to be'). The 'morning' residue is not demonstrably present in the verse — it survives only paradigmatically (أصبح vs أمسى) and etymologically. The lamp cluster (24:35, 41:12, 67:5) is the parallel counterexample from the opposite direction: there the residue is 'bright light', with the time-of-morning component absent. Together these two clusters show the root's invariant splits — one branch keeps the LIGHT, the other keeps the ONSET/TRANSITION — so no single element is transparently visible in literally every occurrence.

byn.candidate_root_contribution: The root contributes DEMARCATION-BETWEEN: the positing of an interval/boundary separating two (or more) referents, and the DISTINCTNESS that this separation produces — one thing set apart from another so that it stands out as itself. The single residue has two co-present faces: (a) the separating interval ("between"), and (b) the distinctness/manifestness that follows from being set apart ("clear, evident, made-plain"). It is inherently dyadic (A demarcated from / against B).
byn.plain_explanation: Every occurrence turns on putting a gap or boundary between two things and thereby making them distinct. The 243 LOC uses (bayna, baynahum, bayna yadayhi, ma baynahuma) foreground the interval itself: 10:29 "between us and you", 15:85 "what is between them" (heavens and earth), 16:66 milk "from between dung and blood", 17:110 "between that" (a middle way), 18:61 the junction "between the two seas", 10:28 "we separated between them" (fazayyalna baynahum). The clarity cluster foregrounds the result of that separation: bayyinah/bayyinat (distinguishing proof, 83x N), bayyin/bayyinat (evident, 19x ADJ), mubin (manifest / that which makes distinct, Form IV, 119x across N(IV)+ADJ(IV)), bayyana (V-II, to set apart = make distinct/explain, 35x), tabayyana (V-V, to become distinct, or to seek the distinction/verify, 18x), abana/yubin (IV, 43:52 barely "makes himself plain" of Moses' speech), istabana/mustabin (X, 6:55 "that the way become clear", 37:117 "the lucid Book"), mubayyinah (II, 4:19/65:1/33:30 a "manifest" indecency = distinctly evident). The two faces are not two roots: 2:187 welds them — "until the white thread becomes DISTINCT (yatabayyana) to you FROM (min) the black thread", and the same verse closes "thus God makes-distinct (yubayyinu) His signs." 2:256 repeats it: "right conduct has become DISTINCT (tabayyana) FROM (min) error." Manifestness in this root is always distinctness-against-a-background, i.e. the same demarcation seen from its epistemic side.
byn.strongest_counterexample: The most bleached uses are the pure locative prepositions — ma baynahuma "what is between them" (15:85), bayna yadayhi "before it/him" (10:37, 13:11), bayna dhalika "between that" (17:110). Here almost nothing but the bare "interval between two" survives; the "distinctness/clarity" face is dormant. This is not a defeater, because the separation face IS the root residue (its other pole), and these uses never denote anything but the demarcating interval — they never drift to an unrelated sense. A second potential resister, tabayyana meaning "verify/ascertain" (49:6, 4:94), is reconciled: to ascertain is to seek the distinction of true from false — the make-distinct residue in an epistemic-imperative construction, confirmed by 2:256/2:187 where tabayyana + min is literally "become distinct from."

Alh.candidate_root_contribution: Deity-hood: the status/category of being a god — an entity set up or invoked as an object of worship. The root names the DEITY-slot itself (the thing that is a god), independent of whether the claim to divinity is affirmed (Allah) or denied (the idols). It is entity-categorial, not the relational lordship of r-b-b nor the worship-act of ʕ-b-d.
Alh.plain_explanation: Every one of the 2851 occurrences is either the common noun ilah / plural aliha ("a deity / deities," 147 = form N) or the proper name Allah / vocative Allahumma ("God," 2704 = form PN). Both surface families denote the same thing at bottom: a being named as a god. Allah is the one true deity (the sole legitimate ilah); the plural aliha are the false gods the idolaters name and worship; the negated singular in "la ilaha illa..." asserts there is no deity but the one; the interrogative "a-ilahun maʕa llah" ("is there a deity alongside Allah?") challenges rival deity-claims. In each, once you subtract case/number, proclitics (wa-, bi-, li-, ta-, fa-), interrogative hamza, and construction, what remains is the same residue: "that which is (taken as) a god."
Alh.strongest_counterexample: The proper name Allah itself (2704 occurrences, ~95% of the data). One can argue a rigid-designator proper name has subtracted its descriptive residue entirely, leaving pure reference — the way "God" as a personal name need not actively predicate "is a deity." If that view is taken, the deity residue is not DEMONSTRABLY present in the bulk of occurrences but only etymologically assumed, and universal presence would rest on an unverifiable claim about a frozen name. This does not surface as an incoherent occurrence (no verse uses Allah to mean anything non-divine), but it is the point where the residue is weakest / least independently observable.

xyr.candidate_root_contribution: The status of being the preferred/superior good: that which is (or would be) singled out over alternatives as the more choiceworthy/beneficial option; and, in the verbal derivations, the act of singling that preferred thing out (to choose/select). Residue = PREFERENCE-OF-THE-GOOD (choiceworthiness).
xyr.plain_explanation: Every kh-y-r word in the set turns on one axis: that which is preferred because it is good (the better, the best, the choiceworthy), and in the verbs the act of singling that out. The comparative khayrun-min ("better than": 38:76 Iblis "I am better than him", 97:3 "better than a thousand months", 2:221, 27:36) names X as the preferred term of a comparison. The construct khayru + genitive-plural ("best of judges/providers/creation": 10:109, 22:58, 98:7; 3:110 khayra ummatin "best community") names the topmost of a class. Bare khayr ("good/benefit/wealth": 100:8 love of khayr, 2:180 "if he leaves khayr", 2:215, 22:36 "in them is khayr for you", 70:21 "khayr touches him") names the desirable-good one loves, spends, is touched by. Khayrat ("good things/deeds": 2:148 and 5:48 "race to the khayrat", 21:90, 23:61, 9:88) names the choiceworthy things one competes for. The verbs (Form VIII ikhtara/ikhtartuka: 20:13, 44:32 "over the worlds", 7:155 "singled out as preferred"; Form V yatakhayyarun/takhayyarun: 56:20, 68:38 "pick what they prefer"; and al-khiyarah: 28:68, 33:36 "the prerogative of choice") enact that same preference as an act of selection. Across all 196 the root supplies the preferred-good; form, construction and context supply the comparison, superlative frame, referent or agency.
xyr.strongest_counterexample: khayru al-makirin "best of schemers" (3:54, 8:30) and Iblis's ana khayrun minhu "I am better than him" (7:12, 38:76). In the first, the class (makr) is not itself morally good, yet the root still contributes "the pre-eminent/most-effective of the class" (superiority/preference), with the valence supplied by context, not the root. In the second, the claim is false, yet the root still contributes an asserted superiority/preferability; the falsehood is contextual, not a different root sense. Neither breaks universal presence: preference-of-the-superior remains the residue.

Hsn.candidate_root_contribution: The root contributes a single positive evaluative quality: the state of being — or the act of rendering — GOOD / FINE / FAIR / COMELY / EXCELLENT. It marks the "good/fine" pole of an evaluative axis whose opposite pole the Quran names with سوء / سيّئة (and, aesthetically, قبح). This one quality surfaces both aesthetically (beauty, comeliness, fairness) and morally/qualitatively (goodness, excellence, best-ness); the two are not separate meanings but the same evaluative fineness applied to appearance versus conduct/outcome.
Hsn.plain_explanation: Every ح-س-ن word in the packet says that something is good/fine, is made good/fine, or is the best/finest. The forms distribute the same core quality across grammatical slots. ADJ حَسَن/حِسَان predicates the quality of a noun: رزقًا حسنًا "goodly provision" (11:88, 16:67, 22:58), خيراتٌ حِسانٌ "fair maidens" (55:70), عبقريٍّ حِسانٍ "fine carpets" (55:76), الأسماء الحُسنى "the finest names" (7:180, 17:110, 20:8, 59:24), أسوةٌ حسنةٌ "a good example" (33:21, 60:4, 60:6), قرضًا حسنًا "a goodly loan" (2:245, 57:11, 64:17, 73:20). N حَسَنة nominalizes it as "a good thing/deed," repeatedly and explicitly opposed to سيّئة (13:22, 41:34, 4:78-79, 27:46, 28:54, 7:168 بالحسنات والسيّئات). The elative أَحْسَن = "better/finest/best" (أحسن القصص 12:3, أحسن الحديث 39:23, أحسن تقويم 95:4, بالتي هي أحسن 6:152/17:34/29:46). The superlative feminine الحُسْنَى = "the best (reward/outcome)" (10:26, 53:31, 92:6/92:9, 4:95, 57:10). حُسْن = "goodness/fineness" (حسنُ مآب 13:29, حُسنُهنّ "their beauty" 33:52). The Form-IV verb أَحْسَن and its verbal noun إِحْسَان = "to make good / to do good / excellence" (أحسن كل شيء خلقه 32:7, فأحسن صوركم 40:64/64:3, أحسن مثواي 12:23, بالوالدين إحسانًا, هل جزاء الإحسان إلا الإحسان 55:60), and the participle مُحْسِن/المُحْسِنِين = "doer(s) of good." The stative Form-I حَسُنَ = "is/became good/excellent" (حَسُنَت مرتفقًا 18:31, حَسُنَت مستقرًّا 25:76, حَسُنَ أولئك رفيقًا 4:69). Subtract the form and the constant is always the good/fine/excellent quality.
Hsn.strongest_counterexample: 18:104 (وهم يحسبون أنهم يُحسنون صُنعًا, "they reckon they are doing good in work") and 35:8 (فرآه حسنًا, an evil deed that its doer "sees as good/fine"). Here the good-quality is FALSELY attributed to something actually bad. This does not break presence: the root still denotes exactly the "good/fine" quality — it is merely predicated wrongly (subjectively claimed/perceived). The word means "good"; the falsehood lies in the predication, not in a shift of the root's contribution. A second, distinctness-testing case is the recurring pairing خيرٌ وأحسن (17:35, 4:59) and أحسن مقيلًا / خير مستقرًّا (25:24), where أحسن can look synonymous with خير — but the very co-occurrence shows the Quran treats them as distinct facets (benefit/welfare = خير, fineness/excellence = أحسن), which supports rather than dissolves the residue.

Tyb.candidate_root_contribution: Root ط ي ب contributes an intrinsic POSITIVE QUALITY of a referent: being wholesome / agreeable / pure / good — pleasing to sense, sound moral judgment, or appetite, and free of contamination or foulness. Its defining anchor is the repeated explicit contrast with خبيث (khabith = foul/corrupt/impure). The residue is NOT "lawful," "beautiful in form," or "sound/fit-for-purpose," but the wholesome-agreeable-pure goodness intrinsic to the thing itself.
Tyb.plain_explanation: Across all 50 occurrences the word tags something as "good" in the sense of clean, wholesome, agreeable and unspoiled. Food/provision is "the good things" (الطيبات) that are wholesome to eat; speech can be "good/pure" (كلمة طيبة, الكلم الطيب, الطيب من القول); a wind is "favorable/pleasant" (ريح طيبة); earth for dry ablution is "clean/pure" (صعيدا طيبا); offspring, a life, dwellings, a land and a greeting are "good/wholesome"; the dying believers are received "in a good/pure state" (طيبين); and the verb طاب means "to be/become good, pleasing, or willingly content." Everywhere the root marks agreeable wholesome purity — the opposite of the foul (خبيث), which stands as its named antonym in six verses.
Tyb.strongest_counterexample: 4:4 فإن طِبْنَ لكم عن شيء منه نفسًا ("if they, of their own good pleasure, remit to you part of it"). Here the root shifts from an intrinsic quality of a thing to the volitional pleasedness/contentment of a self. It is still reconcilable: the residue is the "good/agreeable" state — the self being genuinely well-pleased and willing — the psychological instance of tayyib (cf. نفسًا "as to self"). A related edge case is صعيدا طيبا (4:43, 5:6) where the sense narrows to "ritually clean/pure earth," but purity is a core face of the same residue and is confirmed by the tayyib/khabith purity axis elsewhere. Neither breaks universal presence; both instantiate wholesome-agreeable-pure goodness rather than contradict it.

fsd.candidate_root_contribution: The root contributes the undoing or absence of sound, functioning integrity: the passage of some ordered/wholesome state into ruin, spoilage, breakdown, disorder. It is the counter-state to ص ل ح (soundness/being-set-right). Intransitively it is "to fall into ruin/disorder" (a system losing its working coherence); causatively/agentively it is "to bring to ruin, to spoil, to work corruption." The invariant is not an act of destruction per se but the resulting loss of a sound, integral order.
fsd.plain_explanation: Every one of the 50 occurrences turns on one idea: a sound, working order being spoiled or falling apart — the opposite of things being set right (صلاح). Three verb-forms describe the cosmos itself "going to ruin" if it had multiple gods (21:22, 23:71, 2:251) — pure, agent-free breakdown of ordered functioning. The Form IV verbs and the participle مفسدون/مفسدين describe people who "bring ruin" in the land (spreading disorder, bloodshed, cutting ties, mismanaging orphans' estates). The noun فساد names the ruined state itself ("corruption appeared on land and sea," 30:41). Whether spontaneous (heavens/earth) or caused (people in the earth), the shared residue is: the loss/undoing of a sound, integral order.
fsd.strongest_counterexample: 2:220 (ٱلْمُفْسِدَ مِنَ ٱلْمُصْلِحِ) is the mildest, non-violent case — merely mismanaging/spoiling an orphan's estate, with no "corruption in the land" crime-scene. It could tempt a narrower "large-scale social evil" gloss, but it in fact confirms the residue: the mufsid is precisely the one who spoils/ruins the affair as against the one who sets it right, matching the antonymy exactly. The disciplining case in the other direction is 21:22 لَفَسَدَتَا (heavens and earth "would go to ruin"): it has no moral agent, so it forbids reading the root as "evildoing" and forces the neutral "breakdown of sound order."

nfE.candidate_root_contribution: The bringing-about of benefit/advantage that accrues to a recipient — the positive functional-good pole (usefulness, profit, gain that reaches a beneficiary), standing as the antonymic counterpart of ضرّ (harm).
nfE.plain_explanation: Across all 50 occurrences the root نفع denotes conferring benefit/advantage on someone — something proving useful or profitable to a recipient. This shows up as a verb (يَنْفَع "benefits X"), as an abstract noun (نَفْع "benefit"), and as a concrete plural (مَنَافِع "uses/benefits" — of cattle, iron, wine, the pilgrimage). Whether the statement is positive (faith benefited the town 10:98; the reminder benefits believers 51:55; water/ships that benefit people 13:17, 2:164) or negative (idols that can neither benefit nor harm; intercession/faith/excuse/wealth that will not benefit on the Day), the same nucleus is present: advantage accruing to a beneficiary. Negated cases still fully presuppose the concept — they deny that benefit will materialize, which requires the concept of benefit.
nfE.strongest_counterexample: 57:25 مَنَافِعُ لِلنَّاسِ ("and [in iron] benefits for people"), juxtaposed with بَأْسٌ شَدِيدٌ ("great might"). Here نفع is a concrete plural noun rather than a benefit/harm event, so one might ask whether it has drifted to mere "material commodity." But it holds: مَنَافِع are precisely the useful advantages iron confers on people (لِلنَّاسِ marks the beneficiary), i.e. the reified plural of the same residue. The eschatological negations (e.g. 74:48 شَفَاعَةُ الشَّافِعِينَ that does not benefit) are also non-resistant: they deny the accrual of benefit, which entails the concept.

Eql.candidate_root_contribution: The active mental operation of grasping and connecting input — signs, speech, or consequences — into an intelligible conclusion that ought to govern belief and conduct. Across all 49 occurrences the verb never denotes stored knowledge or a possessed fact; it denotes a *process* that is demanded of, exercised by, or absent in the subject: turning heard/seen/read evidence into a binding comprehension. This is why it recurs in the imperative-rebuke ("do you not then reason?"), the qualifier ("signs for a people who reason"), the purpose clause ("that you may reason"), and the accusation ("they do not reason"). Distinctively, when transitive its object is precisely something to be construed — the word of God (2:75 "after they had comprehended it"), the parables (29:43 "none comprehends them but the learned") — and its located organ is the heart (22:46 "hearts by which they reason"), while it is repeatedly set beside/above mere hearing (10:42, 25:44, 67:10, 2:75). The residue is therefore the connective-comprehending act, not the perception that feeds it nor the knowledge that might result.
Eql.plain_explanation: This root is one word used one way in all 49 places: a verb meaning "to use one's reason / to comprehend." God repeatedly points to natural signs (day and night, rain reviving the earth, sun and moon), to scripture, and to moral facts (the hereafter is better than this life), and then asks whether people "reason" — i.e. whether they actually connect the evidence in front of them to the obvious conclusion. People who fail to do this are compared to cattle (25:44), to the deaf-dumb-blind (2:171, 8:22), and to the worst of beasts (8:22). The word is never about having information; it is about the live act of grasping and joining the dots. That single sense fits every occurrence with no exceptions.
Eql.strongest_counterexample: 29:43 "وَمَا يَعْقِلُهَآ إِلَّا ٱلْعَٰلِمُونَ" — "none reason/comprehend them [the parables] except those who know." This is the strongest tension because it pairs the verb with ٱلْعَٰلِمُونَ (the knowers), risking collapse into "knowledge" (علم). But it in fact confirms the residue: the parables (هَا) are the object to be *construed*, and the verse distinguishes the act of construing them from the class of people (the learned) capable of it — reasoning is the operation, knowledge is the precondition, not the same thing. The other candidate, 22:46 "قُلُوبٌ يَعْقِلُونَ بِهَا" (hearts by which they reason), also holds: it names the organ/instrument of the act without altering the act itself.

$kk.candidate_root_contribution: The root contributes a state of unsettled uncertainty: the mind held in suspension between alternatives, not firmly decided/convinced about the truth of some object-claim. In every occurrence it names a subject's non-settledness regarding a specific matter (a revelation, a religion, the Hereafter, a messenger's call, or God). After subtracting the noun form and its construction, the residue is "wavering / lack of firm conviction about X" — neither knowledge (علم/يقين) nor mere leaning (ظنّ), but an interior non-resolution.
$kk.plain_explanation: Every one of the 15 confirmed occurrences is the noun شَكّ ("doubt"). Fourteen appear in the locative construction (لـ)فِى شَكٍّ — "(they/you are) IN doubt" — treating doubt as a state one is inside of. The remaining one (14:10) is the nominative in a rhetorical question, أَفِى ٱللَّهِ شَكٌّ ("Is there any doubt about God?"), which presupposes there should be none — still the same noun with the same meaning. In each case the object of doubt is introduced by مِن / مِمَّا / مِنْه / مِنْها (about my religion 10:104, about what We sent down 10:94, about it 11:110, about what you call us to 11:62/14:9, about the Hereafter 27:66/34:21, about My reminder 38:8, about what came to you 40:34, about it 41:45/42:14/4:157). Two (34:54, 44:9) leave the object implicit but the context (revelation/the reckoning) is identical. The contribution — being unsettled/uncertain about a truth-claim — is demonstrably present in all 15.
$kk.strongest_counterexample: 14:10 — أَفِى ٱللَّهِ شَكٌّ ("Is there any doubt concerning God?"). This is the only non-فِى-شَكّ-state token: شَكّ is nominative subject of a rhetorical existential question, and its object is God's very reality rather than a revelation/message. It is also the only case where the verse's rhetorical thrust asserts doubt should NOT exist. Yet the lexical contribution is unchanged — the word still denotes uncertainty about a truth, and the rhetorical question only works because شَكّ means exactly "unsettled uncertainty." It does not resist the proposed residue; it confirms it by negation.

Hrj.candidate_root_contribution: An impassable tightness / constriction — a straitening that closes off room to move, breathe, or act. In its most literal packet witness (6:125, صدره ضيقا حرجا) it names an extreme narrowing of the chest; generalized, it is the binding, hemming-in that leaves no give.
Hrj.plain_explanation: The root ح ر ج carries the sense of being hemmed in with no room — a constricting tightness. You see it plainly where the Quran describes a chest made "narrow and حرجا" (6:125) or a constriction "in your chest" (7:2), and an inner tightness/resistance one might "find in oneself" about a judgment (4:65). The large family of legal verses all use the fixed formula "there is no حرج upon so-and-so" — over the blind, lame, sick, the weak, the Prophet, the believers (24:61, 48:17, 9:91, 33:37-50, 22:78, 5:6). There the same core sense operates: no constricting restriction/burden is laid upon them. The formula's "no ... upon" contributes the removal/exemption; the domain (religion, ablution, adoption law) is context; what is left in every case is the notion of a straitening tightness. Even the abstract legal uses read cleanly as "no binding constraint is placed on you," not as a separate meaning.
Hrj.strongest_counterexample: The purely legal-permission verses 33:37, 33:38, 33:50 are the hardest: there "no حرج upon the Prophet/the believers" concerning marrying adopted sons' ex-wives reads most naturally in English as "no blame/sin," which could suggest the root means culpability rather than constriction. However, the constriction reading still fits — the removal of a binding legal restriction that would otherwise hem the person in — and, decisively, 24:61 places حرج and جناح side by side in one verse, showing the Quran does not treat حرج as the blame-word (that is جناح); حرج is the straitening these persons are freed from.

Hrr.candidate_root_contribution: The strongest single candidate contribution is "being unbound / released from bondage or constraint — free." It is demonstrably present in two clusters on internal evidence: (a) al-Hurr / al-Hurr in 2:178, where the free person is explicitly set against al-'abd (the slave), and (b) the Form II tahriru raqabah cluster (4:92 x3, 58:3, 5:89) plus muharraran (3:35), where the act is making a slave-neck free / dedicating-releasing a child to God. Across these 8 occurrences the residue "release from bondage" survives after subtracting form and participants. However, this candidate is NOT present in the remaining 7 occurrences (heat: 16:81, 35:21, 9:81 x2; silk: 22:23, 35:33, 76:12), so it is not a universal contribution.
Hrr.plain_explanation: The root ح ر ر in the Quran breaks into three semantic islands that share only the three consonants, not a single demonstrable meaning: HEAT (al-harr, al-harur, harr — garments that protect from heat, scorching heat, Hellfire's intensity), SILK (harir — the fabric of Paradise), and FREEDOM (al-hurr = a free man vs. a slave; tahriru raqabah = freeing a slave; muharraran = a dedicated/released child). The freedom sense (8 of 15 occurrences) is internally coherent and even self-defines via its antonym 'slave.' But the heat sense (4) and silk sense (3) cannot be reduced to that freedom residue using only the verse evidence — nothing in "garments that guard you from the heat" or "their garment is silk" internally evokes release from bondage. Bridging heat, silk, and freedom would require outside etymology, which the rules forbid as evidence. Because whole clusters resist, universal presence fails.
Hrr.strongest_counterexample: 22:23 / 35:33 / 76:12 — harir (silk), a paradisal luxury fabric. It resists BOTH rival unifying hypotheses simultaneously: it carries no internal sense of "freedom/release" and no internal sense of "heat." A garment described only as fine cloth worn by the blessed offers nothing, on verse-internal grounds, that can be equated with either the free-vs-slave residue or the thermal residue. Silk therefore stands as an irreducible third island and single-handedly blocks universal presence.

Smm.candidate_root_contribution: Closure/imperviousness of the aural channel — the ear sealed shut so that sound, and specifically the call (al-du'a'), does not penetrate or register. The residue is not "not-hearing" as a bare negation but a stopped-up, blocked receptive channel: the sealed state that makes aural reception impossible.
Smm.plain_explanation: Every one of the 15 occurrences means "deaf / made deaf / became deaf." The shared root contribution across all of them is a BLOCKED HEARING CHANNEL — an ear stopped up so sound cannot get in. In 12 places it is the attribute/noun "the deaf" (as-summ, al-asamm, summan). Twice (5:71) it is the verb "they became deaf" (they closed their own ears). Once (47:23) it is causative "He made them deaf." The residue is stable and literal at the sensory level even when the reference is spiritual: disbelievers are likened to people whose ears are sealed to the call. Three times the object is explicitly al-du'a' (the call) — "the deaf do not hear the call" (21:45, 27:80, 30:52), which pins the residue to aural non-reception, not a general dullness.
Smm.strongest_counterexample: 25:73 — "lam yakhirru 'alayha summan wa 'umyanan" ("they do not fall upon them [the ayat] deaf and blind") — here summ describes the manner in which believers do NOT receive revelation. The reference is inverted (a negated/desired non-state) and abstract, so one might argue the sensory core is bleached. But even here the residue holds: the contrast is precisely between an ear sealed to the ayat versus one open to them; "deaf" still contributes blocked aural reception. Likewise 5:71 sammu is fully metaphorical, yet the pattern still denotes entering the sealed-hearing state. Neither dissolves the residue.

$Am.candidate_root_contribution: The root marks the LEFT side construed as the inauspicious / ill-omened / ill-fated direction — "left-handedness" carrying the coloring of doom and misfortune (as opposed to the blessed right). In all occurrences it names the damned cohort via the noun al-mash'amah, literally "the left(-hand side)."
$Am.plain_explanation: Every one of the 3 confirmed occurrences is the exact same word — الْمَشْـَٔمَة (al-mash'amah, maf'alah pattern) — in the exact same genitive phrase أَصْحَٰبُ الْمَشْـَٔمَةِ "the companions of the left/ill-omen." In 56:9 it appears twice (the emphatic doubling أصحاب المشأمة ما أصحاب المشأمة), and in 90:19 it labels those who disbelieved in God's signs. Across all three the word designates the doomed group placed on the ill-fated left side at the reckoning, in explicit or implicit contrast with أصحاب الميمنة ("the companions of the right", from the antonym root ي م ن). The root's contribution — the left as the ominous, damnation-marked direction — is present in every occurrence. However, because the evidence is a single word-type in a single construction repeated three times, the contribution cannot be tested across formal or contextual variation.
$Am.strongest_counterexample: There is no dissenting occurrence — but the strongest challenge is structural rather than a counterexample: all 3 tokens are one and the same lexeme (المشأمة) in one and the same construction (أصحاب المشأمة). Universal presence is therefore satisfied trivially, because there is only one word-type to satisfy it. No occurrence exercises a different form, a different collocation, or a non-eschatological sense, so the residue is never stress-tested. The nearest thing to a tension is 90:19, where the ill-omen coloring is discharged entirely by the surrounding كَفَرُوا clause, leaving open whether المشأمة itself contributes "ill-omen" or merely "left/the-left-group" with omen supplied contextually.

$Hn.candidate_root_contribution: Loading up / freighting to capacity — the act or resultant state of a vessel being packed with its cargo and passengers. The root residue is "being laden/freighted": filled by having a load put into it, not merely spatially full.
$Hn.plain_explanation: The root ش ح ن occurs in the Quran only three times, and in every case it is the same word: مَشْحُون, the passive participle describing الفلك (the ship) — "the laden ship." In 26:119 it is Noah's ark that saves him and those with him; in 36:41 it is the loaded ship carrying people's offspring as a sign; in 37:140 it is the ship Jonah flees to. Across all three the ship is characterized as loaded/freighted — packed with its load of people (and by narrative implication provisions/animals). The root's contribution across the full set is the notion of being loaded up to full capacity.
$Hn.strongest_counterexample: There is no resistant occurrence — all three tokens are the literally identical word مَشْحُون. The real weakness is not a counterexample but the total absence of variation: the root never appears outside الفلك المشحون, so nothing tests whether the residue is "loading with freight" specifically versus a more generic "filled/full." A hostile reading could claim the three tokens are one frozen lexical fossil, not evidence of a productive root contribution.

$TT.candidate_root_contribution: A departure that overshoots remotely far beyond the correct/proper limit — the spatial "far edge" sense (cf. shaṭṭ, the far riverbank) generalized to a bound of truth, justice, or measure. The residue is: going too far past the right mark.
$TT.plain_explanation: Across all 3 occurrences the root marks something that has gone far beyond the proper bound. In 18:14 and 72:4 it is a statement (object of a speech verb) that overshoots the truth about God — an extreme, far-fetched falsehood. In 38:22 it is a verb (Form IV) asking a judge not to overshoot the standard of just judgment ("judge with truth and do not shaṭaṭ"). Speech-excess vs. judicial-excess are different domains, but the same core "far past the correct limit" is present in each.
$TT.strongest_counterexample: 38:22 (تُشْطِط) is the hardest: read loosely it could mean simply "be unjust," collapsing the root into ظلم/جور and losing distinctiveness. But its pairing with "احكم بالحق" (judge with the truth) frames it as overshooting/deviating far from the truth-standard, preserving the "far beyond the mark" residue rather than a generic "do wrong." It reconciles.

$kw.candidate_root_contribution: The act of laying open / pouring out an inner distress or grievance and directing it outward toward a recipient for relief. Derived from the two verbal occurrences: 12:86 أَشْكُوا۟ (Form I) explicitly pairs the act with its inner object بَثِّى وَحُزْنِى ("my anguish and grief") and the recipient إِلَى ٱللَّهِ; 58:1 تَشْتَكِى (Form VIII) shows the same directional structure إِلَى ٱللَّهِ over a marital grievance. The residue after subtracting form and the إلى-recipient construction is: exposing-what-is-held-within-as-a-grievance to another.
$kw.plain_explanation: This root's clear meaning is "to complain / voice a grievance" — to take an inner pain or wrong and lay it open before someone who can address it. Both verb occurrences do exactly this, and both direct the complaint "to Allah" (إلى الله): Jacob pouring out his grief (12:86), and the woman appealing over her husband (58:1). The problem is the third occurrence, 24:35, which is not a verb of complaining at all but the noun مِشكاة — a "niche" or recess in a wall that holds a lamp. A niche has no grievance, no one complaining, and no recipient. To make the niche "fit" the complaint sense you have to reach outside the packet (to classical lexica about شكوة as a receptacle/waterskin, or to the loanword hypothesis for mishkāt), which the rules forbid as evidence. So the crisp contribution proven in two of three occurrences is genuinely absent from the third, and I cannot honestly claim universal presence.
$kw.strongest_counterexample: 24:35 كَمِشْكَوٰةٍ فِيهَا مِصْبَاحٌ — the noun مِشكاة is a lamp-niche/recess. Under the candidate contribution ("lay open an inner grievance to a recipient") there is nothing to reconcile: no complainant, no grievance, no directed appeal, and no addressee who grants relief. The only way to bridge it to the complaint sense is to substitute a far more abstract notion ("a hollow/receptacle that holds and presents its content outward") and then re-read the verbs through that abstraction — but that shift is post-hoc, leans on external lexicography (شكوة = waterskin) and on the contested loanword status of mishkāt, both of which are inadmissible as packet-internal evidence. The grievance residue is therefore falsifiably absent here.

$nA.candidate_root_contribution: Active detestation/aversion directed at a human target — an affectively charged hatred that spurns and rejects its object (person or group), tilting toward hostile impulse rather than neutral dislike.
$nA.plain_explanation: All three occurrences of ش ن ا name hatred/detestation aimed at people. In 108:3 the active participle شانئك is "the one who detests you" — a personal enemy defined by his hatred. In 5:2 and 5:8 the verbal noun شنآن قوم is "detestation of a people," a feeling the believers are warned not to let drive them into transgression or injustice. Whether realized as the agent (the hater) or the abstract affect (the hating), the constant contribution is directed, active hatred toward a human target.
$nA.strongest_counterexample: 5:2 شنآن قوم أن صدوكم — here the hatred has a stated cause (their having barred you from the Sacred Mosque), so one might read the word as "grievance/resentment over a wrong" rather than pure hatred. But the syntax makes شنآن the emotion that could "drive you to transgress," i.e., a detestation of the people that must be restrained; the cause-clause modifies why the hatred exists, not what the word means. Residue holds.
